claim: ASAP2s is a novel voltage indicator with improved sensitivity compared to ASAP1.
source: Here, we report ASAP2s, a novel voltage indicator with improved sensitivity.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding, and subsequent data in the manuscript demonstrates improved sensitivity metrics.

claim: ASAP2s enables robust single-trial detection of action potentials in organotypic slice cultures using random-access multi-photon microscopy.
source: By imaging ASAP2s using random-access multi-photon microscopy, we demonstrate robust single-trial detection of action potentials in organotypic slice cultures.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: ASAP2s enables two-photon imaging of graded potentials in organotypic slice cultures and in Drosophila.
source: We also show that ASAP2s enables two-photon imaging of graded potentials in organotypic slice cultures and in Drosophila.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this capability, supported by experimental demonstrations in the results.

claim: The combination of ASAP2s and fast two-photon imaging methods enables detection of neural electrical activity with subcellular spatial resolution and millisecond-timescale precision.
source: These results demonstrate that the combination of ASAP2s and fast two-photon imaging methods enables detection of neural electrical activity with subcellular spatial resolution and millisecond-timescale precision.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Genetically encoded calcium indicators are commonly used to detect forms of neuronal activity that trigger calcium flux into neurons.
source: Genetically encoded calcium indicators are commonly used to detect the forms of neuronal activity that trigger calcium flux into neurons (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012; Tian et al., 2012; Lin and Schnitzer, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: GCaMP6f can detect single action potentials in cell bodies and synaptic responses in spines.
source: For example, recent calcium indicators such as GCaMP6f can detect single action potentials (APs) in cell bodies and synaptic responses in spines (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Calcium concentration is not directly related to membrane potential.
source: However, calcium concentration is not directly related to membrane potential, and therefore cannot be used to follow voltage changes that do not result in substantial calcium fluxes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the relationship between calcium and voltage.

claim: Calcium indicators cannot effectively report hyperpolarizations and somatic subthreshold depolarizations in many neuronal cell types.
source: Calcium indicators thus cannot effectively report hyperpolarizations and somatic subthreshold depolarizations in many neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that calcium concentration is not directly related to membrane potential and that these voltage changes do not result in substantial calcium fluxes.

claim: The slow kinetics of calcium indicators and calcium transients limit their ability to report voltage changes with high temporal precision and to track fast trains of action potentials.
source: The slow kinetics of calcium indicators and of calcium transients also limit the ability of calcium indicators to report voltage changes with high temporal precision and to track fast trains of action potentials (Koester and Sakmann, 2000,Helmchen et al., 1996; Theis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genetically encoded voltage indicators (GEVIs) have been developed to monitor transmembrane voltage rather than calcium concentration.
source: To follow membrane potential dynamics more accurately, fluorescent indicators that monitor transmembrane voltage rather than calcium concentration have been developed (Lin and Schnitzer, 2016; Knöpfel et al., 2015; Yang and St-Pierre, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: GEVIs have been used to image activity of neuronal populations in vivo using widefield one-photon illumination.
source: These genetically encoded voltage indicators (GEVIs) have been used to image activity of neuronal populations in vivo (Akemann et al., 2010, 2012; Scott et al., 2014; Carandini et al., 2015; Mutoh et al., 2015; Shimaoka et al., 2017) and of single neurons within intact brain tissue (Ahrens et al., 2012; Akemann et al., 2013; Flytzanis et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2014, 2015; Storace et al., 2015) using widefield one-photon illumination.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Two-photon microscopy is the preferred modality for in vivo studies because it allows imaging with deeper tissue penetration and with lower background fluorescence and phototoxicity outside of the focal point.
source: However, two-photon microscopy is the preferred modality for in vivo studies as it allows imaging with deeper tissue penetration and with lower background fluorescence and phototoxicity outside of the focal point (Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006; Prevedel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on two-photon microscopy.

claim: GEVI-based voltage imaging in intact tissue with two-photon excitation has only been demonstrated with either low temporal resolution, low spatial resolution, or both.
source: GEVI-based voltage imaging in intact tissue with two-photon excitation has only been demonstrated for monitoring neural activity with either low temporal resolution (less than 100 Hz), low spatial resolution (averaging over ensembles of cells), or both (Ahrens et al., 2012; Akemann et al., 2013; Storace et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and establishes the gap that the current work addresses.

claim: Robust single-trial two-photon GEVI imaging with millisecond-timescale and cellular or subcellular resolution in intact neuronal tissue has not yet been reported prior to this study.
source: Robust single-trial two-photon GEVI imaging with millisecond-timescale and cellular or subcellular resolution in intact neuronal tissue has not yet been reported.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the current work by indicating what has not been achieved before.

claim: The probability of correctly identifying spikes from optical noise is higher for sensors with larger response amplitudes, greater brightness, and longer signal decay.
source: The probability of correctly identifying spikes from optical noise is higher for sensors with larger response amplitudes, greater brightness, and longer signal decay (slower off-rate) (Wilt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilt et al., 2013.

claim: ASAP2s contains an R415Q mutation in the fourth helix (S4) of the voltage-sensing domain.
source: ASAP1 with an R415Q mutation, which neutralizes one of these sensing charges (Figure 1B) met two of our key design criteria: improved voltage responsiveness in HEK293A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and a slower off-rate than ASAP1 (Table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the mutation, and Figure 1B shows the location of the mutation.

claim: ASAP2s exhibits improved voltage responsiveness in HEK293A cells compared to ASAP1.
source: ASAP1 with an R415Q mutation, which neutralizes one of these sensing charges (Figure 1B) met two of our key design criteria: improved voltage responsiveness in HEK293A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and a slower off-rate than ASAP1 (Table 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1I which shows the data.

claim: ASAP2s has a slower off-rate than ASAP1.
source: ASAP1 with an R415Q mutation, which neutralizes one of these sensing charges (Figure 1B) met two of our key design criteria: improved voltage responsiveness in HEK293A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and a slower off-rate than ASAP1 (Table 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Table 1 which contains the kinetic data.

claim: In response to a 1 s, 100 mV depolarization from –70 mV in HEK293A cells, ASAP2s exhibited a steady-state fluorescence change of –38.7 ± 1.1%.
source: In response to a 1 s, 100 mV depolarization from –70 mV in HEK293A cells, ASAP2s exhibited a steady-state fluorescence change of –38.7 ± 1.1%, versus –23.3 ± 1.1% for ASAP1 (mean ± standard error of the mean, p<0.001, t-test), a 66% improvement (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Figure 1C,D which shows the data.

claim: ASAP1 exhibited a steady-state fluorescence change of –23.3 ± 1.1% in response to a 1 s, 100 mV depolarization from –70 mV in HEK293A cells.
source: In response to a 1 s, 100 mV depolarization from –70 mV in HEK293A cells, ASAP2s exhibited a steady-state fluorescence change of –38.7 ± 1.1%, versus –23.3 ± 1.1% for ASAP1 (mean ± standard error of the mean, p<0.001, t-test), a 66% improvement (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Figure 1C,D which shows the data.

claim: ASAP2s shows a 66% improvement in steady-state response amplitude compared to ASAP1.
source: In response to a 1 s, 100 mV depolarization from –70 mV in HEK293A cells, ASAP2s exhibited a steady-state fluorescence change of –38.7 ± 1.1%, versus –23.3 ± 1.1% for ASAP1 (mean ± standard error of the mean, p<0.001, t-test), a 66% improvement (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage improvement based on the measured data.

claim: The steady-state response of ASAP2s to voltage steps has the largest amplitude among GEVIs based on fluorescent proteins.
source: The steady-state response of ASAP2s to voltage steps has the largest amplitude among GEVIs based on fluorescent proteins, surpassing ArcLight Q239 (−32 to −35%, [Jin et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014]), MacQ-mCitrine (~−20%, [Gong et al., 2014]), and Ace2N-mNeon (<-5% steady-state, ~−19% peak, [Gong et al., 2015]).
evidence: The text makes this comparative claim and supports it with citations to published data on other GEVIs.

claim: The fast depolarization time constant (on-rate) of ASAP2s is 5.2 ms.
source: The fast depolarization time constants (on-rates) were 5.2 ms for ASAP2s and 2.9 ms for ASAP1 (Table 1), much faster than the 20 ms for ArcLight.
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Table 1.

claim: The fast depolarization time constant (on-rate) of ASAP1 is 2.9 ms.
source: The fast depolarization time constants (on-rates) were 5.2 ms for ASAP2s and 2.9 ms for ASAP1 (Table 1), much faster than the 20 ms for ArcLight.
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Table 1.

claim: The fast depolarization time constant (on-rate) of ArcLight is 20 ms.
source: The fast depolarization time constants (on-rates) were 5.2 ms for ASAP2s and 2.9 ms for ASAP1 (Table 1), much faster than the 20 ms for ArcLight.
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Table 1.

claim: ASAP2s' fast response to repolarization (fast off-rate) was 24 ms, approximately 10-fold slower than ASAP1.
source: Critically, ASAP2s' fast response to repolarization (fast off-rate) was 24 ms or ~10 fold slower than ASAP1 (Table 1), a useful change for improving spike detection (Wilt et al., 2013), while being still sufficiently rapid to track fast trains of AP waveforms at 100 Hz in single trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The text provides the measurement and references Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: ASAP2s can track fast trains of AP waveforms at 100 Hz in single trials.
source: Critically, ASAP2s' fast response to repolarization (fast off-rate) was 24 ms or ~10 fold slower than ASAP1 (Table 1), a useful change for improving spike detection (Wilt et al., 2013), while being still sufficiently rapid to track fast trains of AP waveforms at 100 Hz in single trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The text states this capability and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1J which shows the data.

claim: ASAP2s matches the brightness of ASAP1 under both one- and two-photon illumination when expressed in HEK293-Kir2.1 cells.
source: When expressed in these cells, ASAP2s matched the brightness of ASAP1 under both one- and two-photon illumination (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B which shows the data.

claim: ASAP1 and ASAP2s are maximally excited at approximately 920 nm under two-photon illumination.
source: Two-photon microscopy experiments were performed by exciting GEVIs at ~920 nm, the wavelength at which ASAP1 and ASAP2s are maximally excited (Figure 1E).
evidence: The text states this and references Figure 1E which shows the two-photon excitation spectra.

claim: EGFP produces maximal brightness when excited at 920 nm under two-photon illumination.
source: The commonly-used fluorescent protein EGFP, which we evaluated as a standard, also produced maximal brightness when excited at 920 nm, consistent with previous reports (Drobizhev et al., 2011).
evidence: The text states this finding and cites a previous report.

claim: Under one-photon widefield microscopy at identical illumination power, ASAP1 and ASAP2s photobleached similarly to each other and to ArcLight.
source: Under one-photon widefield microscopy at identical illumination power, ASAP1 and ASAP2s photobleached similarly to each other and to ArcLight and more slowly than ASAP1::EGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B which shows the photobleaching data.

claim: ASAP1 and ASAP2s photobleached more slowly than ASAP1::EGFP under one-photon widefield microscopy.
source: Under one-photon widefield microscopy at identical illumination power, ASAP1 and ASAP2s photobleached similarly to each other and to ArcLight and more slowly than ASAP1::EGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B which shows the photobleaching data.

claim: A partial recovery in ASAP1 and ASAP2s fluorescence was observed following incubation in darkness.
source: We observed a partial recovery in ASAP1 and ASAP2s fluorescence following incubation in darkness (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–F), possibly due to dark reversion of bleached to unbleached molecules (Sinnecker et al., 2005), diffusion of unbleached probes to the illuminated area, or both (Pincet et al., 2016).
evidence: The text states this observation and references figures showing the data, along with citations to possible mechanisms.

claim: Longer dark incubation resulted in greater fluorescence recovery for ASAP indicators.
source: Longer dark incubation resulted in greater fluorescence recovery, yielding 8.9 ± 0.6% recovery of the original fluorescence for a 0.5 min incubation, and 22.4 ± 0.7% for a 5-min incubation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: The text provides specific measurements and references figures showing the data.

claim: Under two-photon laser scanning excitation, ASAP1 and ASAP2s rapidly lost approximately 30% of their initial brightness but then bleached at slower or similar rates compared with ArcLight and ASAP1::EGFP.
source: Under two-photon laser scanning excitation, ASAP1 and ASAP2s rapidly lost ~30% of their initial brightness but then bleached at slower or similar rates compared with ArcLight and ASAP1::EGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B which shows the photobleaching data.

claim: Incubation in the dark resulted in 20–25% fluorescence recovery of original fluorescence following a 5-min dark incubation for both ASAP1 and ASAP2s under two-photon illumination.
source: Incubation in the dark resulted in fluorescence recovery, as observed under one-photon illumination: 20–25% of original fluorescence was recovered following a 5-min dark incubation for both ASAP1 and ASAP2s and across two conditions with distinct laser power (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F,G).
evidence: The text provides the measurement and references figures showing the data.

claim: The response amplitude of ASAP2s to cardiac potentials in human embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes was –45.1 ± 1.5%.
source: Consistent with our results in HEK293A cells, the response amplitude of ASAP2s to cardiac potentials was greater than that of the other indicators, reaching –45.1 ± 1.5% compared with –24.0 ± 1.8% for ASAP1 and –32.9 ± 1.8% for ArcLight (Figure 2A–D, Video 1).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Figure 2A–D and Video 1.

claim: The response amplitude of ASAP1 to cardiac potentials in human embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes was –24.0 ± 1.8%.
source: Consistent with our results in HEK293A cells, the response amplitude of ASAP2s to cardiac potentials was greater than that of the other indicators, reaching –45.1 ± 1.5% compared with –24.0 ± 1.8% for ASAP1 and –32.9 ± 1.8% for ArcLight (Figure 2A–D, Video 1).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Figure 2A–D and Video 1.

claim: The response amplitude of ArcLight to cardiac potentials in human embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes was –32.9 ± 1.8%.
source: Consistent with our results in HEK293A cells, the response amplitude of ASAP2s to cardiac potentials was greater than that of the other indicators, reaching –45.1 ± 1.5% compared with –24.0 ± 1.8% for ASAP1 and –32.9 ± 1.8% for ArcLight (Figure 2A–D, Video 1).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references Figure 2A–D and Video 1.

claim: The faster kinetics of the ASAP indicators compared to ArcLight enabled a shorter time to peak when reporting cardiac action potentials.
source: The faster kinetics of the ASAP indicators compared to ArcLight enabled a shorter time to peak when reporting cardiac action potentials (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: ASAP2s is well localized at the plasma membrane in cultured rat cortical neurons.
source: We observed that ASAP2s localized efficiently to the plasma membrane in cultured neurons (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), as previously reported with ASAP1 (St-Pierre et al., 2014).
evidence: The text states this observation and references Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 which show confocal images.

claim: In neuronal cultures, ASAP2s reported APs with a –12.2 ± 0.5% fluorescence change.
source: Indeed, in neuronal cultures, ASAP2s reported APs with a –12.2 ± 0.5% fluorescence change, compared with –8.6 ± 0.3% for ASAP1, a 42% improvement in response amplitude (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references figures showing the data.

claim: In neuronal cultures, ASAP1 reported APs with a –8.6 ± 0.3% fluorescence change.
source: Indeed, in neuronal cultures, ASAP2s reported APs with a –12.2 ± 0.5% fluorescence change, compared with –8.6 ± 0.3% for ASAP1, a 42% improvement in response amplitude (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurement and references figures showing the data.

claim: ASAP2s shows a 42% improvement in response amplitude compared to ASAP1 when reporting APs in neuronal cultures.
source: Indeed, in neuronal cultures, ASAP2s reported APs with a –12.2 ± 0.5% fluorescence change, compared with –8.6 ± 0.3% for ASAP1, a 42% improvement in response amplitude (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage improvement based on the measured data.

claim: ASAP2s' responses to APs in neuronal cultures were longer in duration than ASAP1's responses.
source: ASAP2s' responses were also longer in duration (Figure 2J), consistent with its slower kinetics of repolarization.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2J which shows the data.

claim: The combination of higher response amplitude and longer response duration resulted in a 90% greater integrated fluorescence change with ASAP2s than with ASAP1 in neuronal cultures.
source: The combination of higher response amplitude and longer response duration resulted in a 90% greater integrated fluorescence change with ASAP2s than with ASAP1 (Figure 2K).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2K which shows the data.

claim: L2 neurons are monopolar cells of the lamina that receive direct inputs from the R1-6 photoreceptors in Drosophila.
source: Along with L1 and L3, L2 neurons are monopolar cells of the lamina that receive direct inputs from the R1-6 photoreceptors (Figure 3A) (Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Sanes and Zipursky, 2010).
evidence: The text states this anatomical fact and cites published literature.

claim: L2 axon terminals transiently depolarize to light decrements and transiently hyperpolarize to light increments.
source: The fluorescence responses of both ASAP1 and ASAP2s indicated that L2 axon terminals transiently depolarize to light decrements and transiently hyperpolarize to light increments (Figure 3B), consistent with electrophysiological recordings in lamina monopolar cells (Zettler and Järvilehto, 1971) and our prior GEVI-imaging experiments (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The text states this finding, references Figure 3B, and cites supporting literature.

claim: ASAP2s produced significantly larger mean responses than ASAP1 in Drosophila L2 neurons (a 37% increase in amplitude for depolarizations and a 39% increase in amplitude for hyperpolarizations).
source: In line with our in vitro observations, ASAP2s produced significantly larger mean responses than ASAP1 (a 37% increase in amplitude for depolarizations and a 39% increase in amplitude for hyperpolarizations) but was slightly slower (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The text provides the specific measurements and references Figure 3C,D which shows the data.

claim: ASAP2s was slightly slower than ASAP1 in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: In line with our in vitro observations, ASAP2s produced significantly larger mean responses than ASAP1 (a 37% increase in amplitude for depolarizations and a 39% increase in amplitude for hyperpolarizations) but was slightly slower (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3C,D which shows the data.

claim: ArcLight produced fluorescence responses with amplitudes similar to ASAP1 but smaller than ASAP2s in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: We found that ArcLight produced fluorescence responses with amplitudes similar to ASAP1 but smaller than ASAP2s (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3B,D which shows the data.

claim: The kinetics of ArcLight fluorescence changes were significantly slower than those of both ASAP2s and ASAP1 in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: The kinetics of ArcLight fluorescence changes were significantly slower than those of both ASAP2s and ASAP1 (Figure 3D), in agreement with their respective response kinetics in cultured cells (Table 1, Figure 2B,C,E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3D and other figures showing kinetic data.

claim: Over 30 min of continuous illumination, the photostability of ASAP1, ASAP2s, and ArcLight was comparable in Drosophila L2 neurons, with all three indicators bleaching to approximately 30% of their initial brightness.
source: Over 30 min of continuous illumination, the photostability of ASAP1, ASAP2s, and ArcLight was comparable, with all three indicators bleaching to ~30% of their initial brightness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B which shows the photobleaching data.

claim: All three indicators (ASAP1, ASAP2s, and ArcLight) enabled imaging of L2 voltage dynamics with a high signal-to-noise ratio for over 30 min in Drosophila.
source: All three indicators enabled imaging of L2 voltage dynamics with a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for over 30 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1C which shows the data.

claim: Ace2N-2AA-mNeon produced minimal responses to visual stimulation in Drosophila L2 neurons under two-photon illumination.
source: Both indicators fluoresced brightly with two-photon excitation in L2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), but produced minimal (Ace2N-2AA-mNeon) or undetectable (MacQ-mCitrine) responses to visual stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: MacQ-mCitrine produced undetectable responses to visual stimulation in Drosophila L2 neurons under two-photon illumination.
source: Both indicators fluoresced brightly with two-photon excitation in L2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), but produced minimal (Ace2N-2AA-mNeon) or undetectable (MacQ-mCitrine) responses to visual stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references figures showing the data.

claim: The response polarity of Ace2N-2AA-mNeon was inverted under two-photon illumination compared to its response under one-photon illumination.
source: Unexpectedly, the response polarity of Ace2N-2AA-mNeon was inverted compared to its response under one-photon illumination (Gong et al., 2015), an observation robust to excitation wavelength between 920 and 1010 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).

claim: The peak response amplitude of GCaMP6f was substantially larger than that of any of the voltage sensors in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: The peak response amplitude of GCaMP6f was substantially larger than that of any of the voltage sensors, and its single-cell and single-trial responses had correspondingly higher SNR (Figure 3B).

claim: The GCaMP6f response was not transient, continuing to rise or fall during the entire duration of the flash in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: However, the GCaMP6f response was not transient, continuing to rise or fall during the entire duration of the flash.
evidence: The text states this observation about the kinetics of the GCaMP6f response.

claim: The observed calcium indicator traces do not correlate with GEVI traces in a simple manner in Drosophila L2 neurons.
source: Importantly, the observed calcium indicator traces do not correlate with GEVI traces in a simple manner, illustrating the difficulty of using calcium imaging to infer voltage dynamics.
